position: Every event in this log must say WHO acted (person, agent, trigger, connection, scheduler), under WHICH capability (the shell CID that decided), and WHAT was decided, including denials and mocks, because an audit log that only records successes cannot answer 'what was attempted'. Today sign-in is by name only, tokens sit in plaintext in users.json, the first visitor becomes admin, SetUserShell and SetSecret leave no trace beyond an in-memory span, and an unsecured webhook accepts anyone. Moving to immutable events is the chance to fix that, but it also creates new risks: secret values, Fetch responses and personal chat text become permanent unless we design for redaction (references, digests, crypto-shredding) from the first event.

events.why: the first-admin moment must be an explicit, one-time, recorded event (bootstrap token), not 'whoever signs in first'
today a name alone creates an account; the event should record the identity provider and verified subject, never the token
authentication is security relevant; record method and session id hash, never the cookie value
failed authentications are needed to detect brute force and token guessing
users.json tokens never expire today; revocation must exist and be auditable
admin is the strongest privilege; granting it must be explicit, by a named admin, reviewable
symmetry with grant, and the last admin must not be removable without recovery
SetUserShell changes capabilities; record actor, target, old shell CID and new shell CID
privilege escalation could be a request awaiting a second admin's approval rather than immediate
a shell is code; changing a gate in cloud.eyg changes everyone holding it, so record the new shell CID and diff
the policy every program in a channel runs under; must be reviewable as a privilege change
SetWorkspaceSource rewrites every policy, secret binding and connection at once; record author and old/new source CID
an effect the gate allowed; record the shell CID, effect label and digest of the (possibly modified) input
Pass(modified) lets a gate change the input; the original and rewritten input digests both matter for audit
a mock is a decision that the program believes succeeded; it must be recorded as carefully as a pass, with the mocked value
'not allowed by policy' is the evidence of attempted overreach by an agent or script
a crashing gate fails closed today; that is a security-relevant fault, not just an error
durable execution needs it; it must be redacted or encrypted where the result may contain secrets or personal data
replay feeds recorded results back; record which node and that it verified the program CID before resuming
SetSecret must emit name, version, actor and a keyed fingerprint, never the value (the value goes to a vault, not the log)
rotation needs history to know which runs used which version
deletion is a privilege action and must be auditable
network secrets are swapped in for allowed hosts; record secret name+version, host and run, so use is auditable without the value
a Fetch carrying a placeholder to a non-allowed host is a likely exfiltration attempt
only config reads secrets; each read during workspace evaluation should still be counted
@name resolves to the latest version, which is mutable; the event pins the CID actually run
code fetched by hash should have its signatory and hash checked before evaluation
a hash mismatch or unknown signer must stop the run and be visible
record which method passed (HMAC header, bearer, query token) since query tokens leak into logs and proxies
invalid signatures are attacks or misconfiguration; today only a 401 is returned
no timestamp or delivery-id check exists; a duplicate signed body should be detected and recorded
a Webhook without a secret accepts anyone who knows the URL; that choice should be explicit and flagged
Slack/Discord/WhatsApp tokens and app secrets need the same lifecycle as secrets
a subagent inherits the channel shell; delegation is a capability hand-off and should name parent run
AddTrigger gives a program a persistent foothold that outlives the session; who added it and with what script CID
sharing makes channel content public; who shared, with whom, and revocation
dataclips run with their own, possibly broader shell; a controlled privilege boundary crossing
Bind lets a person act inside a channel; record user and the shell actually used
right to erasure: destroy the per-subject key so their messages in immutable events become unreadable (crypto-shredding)
periodic hash-chain or Merkle checkpoint so tampering with the event store is detectable

hotspots.text: Authentication today is a name typed into a form and the first visitor becomes admin. What is the identity of a person, an agent, a trigger and a connection in events, and who bootstraps the first admin?

Recording effect inputs/results for durable execution will put secrets in the log: SetSecret carries the value, Fetch responses can echo tokens, WriteFile can contain credentials. Which effect payloads are stored by reference, encrypted, or redacted, and who holds the keys?

On replay, do we re-run gates against the CURRENT shell or trust the recorded decision? If the shell was tightened (or a secret revoked) after the crash, replaying an old Pass silently continues with privileges that no longer exist.

Right to erasure vs immutable events: chat Posted/Reacted events and webhook bodies contain personal data. Do we need per-subject (or per-channel) encryption keys from day one so erasure is key destruction rather than rewriting history?

Webhooks: no secret means open to the world, the query-token option leaks the secret into URLs and access logs, there is no replay window, and the WhatsApp verify_token uses plain == rather than secure_compare. Should unauthenticated webhooks be forbidden or require an explicit opt-in event?
@name resolves to latest at run time. Should every run pin the resolved CID and verify signature before evaluation, and who is trusted as a signatory for a workspace?

Privilege changes (SetUserShell, SetWorkspaceSource, ChannelShell changes, admin) apply immediately when a holder of the right gate calls them, including an agent in a channel with the admin shell. Do we need two-person approval or at least a 'human only' restriction for these commands?

Traces are capped at 2000 in memory and show 'mock'/'unavailable' only as span attributes. Denials and mocks must become first-class durable events, but with high volume how do we keep them without leaking inputs?
